Introduction and meaning
Assault. BNS restatement of IPC 351. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 351. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 130 is the rule on “Assault”. The section provides that whoever makes any gesture, or any preparation intending or knowing it to be likely that such gesture or preparation will cause any person present to apprehend that he who makes that gesture or preparation is about to use criminal force to that person, is said to commit an assault. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 130 exists so that “Assault” has a closed legal test in Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Homicide, organised crime, terrorism, hurt, acid, restraint, assault, kidnapping and trafficking.

The provision in detail
130. Whoever makes any gesture, or any preparation intending or knowing it to be likely that such gesture or preparation will cause any person present to apprehend that he who makes that gesture or preparation is about to use criminal force to that person, is said to commit an assault

Essential ingredients
1. Whoever makes any gesture, or any preparation intending or knowing it to be likely that such gesture or preparation will cause any person present to apprehend that he who makes that gesture or preparation is about to use criminal force to that person, is said to commit an assault

Statutory illustrations
Illustration (a). A shakes his fist at Z, intending or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby cause Z to believe that A is about to strike Z. A has committed an assault

Exam use: quote illustration (a), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 130 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

Illustration (b). A begins to unloose the muzzle of a ferocious dog, intending or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby cause Z to believe that he is about to cause the dog to attack Z. A has committed an assault upon Z

Exam use: quote illustration (b), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 130 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

Illustration (c). A takes up a stick, saying to Z, “I will give you a beating”. Here, though the words used by A could in no case amount to an assault, and though the mere gesture, unaccompanied by any other circumstances, might not amount to an assault, the gesture explained by the words may amount to an assault

Exam use: quote illustration (c), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 130 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

Explanations
Explanation.—Mere words do not amount to an assault. But the words which a person uses may give to his gestures or preparation such a meaning as may make those gestures or preparations amount to an assault

hypotheticals.question: Whether BNS s. 130 (Assault) applies, and how structured written arguments should be framed.
hypotheticals.analysis:
Step 1 — Identify the provision. The correct current-law cite is BNS s. 130 (Assault), Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body.
Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:
   (1) Whoever makes any gesture, or any preparation intending or knowing it to be likely that such gesture or preparation will cause any person present to apprehend that he who makes that gesture or preparation is about to use criminal force to that person, is said to commit an assault
Step 3 — Read every Explanation. An explanation is part of the section. Omitting it leaves the analysis incomplete and vulnerable to rebuttal.
Step 4 — Map each fact to an ingredient. Write “this fact proves ingredient (a)” or “this fact is missing, so the section is not made out”.
Step 5 — Conclude. If every essential ingredient is proved and no exception covers the case, BNS s. 130 applies. If any essential ingredient fails, say so and stop. Do not invent a different section to save the answer.

learningObjectives: Master the definition of assault under BNS s. 130 as an inchoate apprehension of criminal force.
Analyze the gesture or preparation requirement and the victim's reasonable apprehension.
Understand the statutory Explanation: mere words do not amount to assault, but words may give color to gestures.
Differentiate assault from criminal force and simple hurt.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 130 defines assault as making any gesture or any preparation intending or knowing it to be likely that such gesture or preparation will cause any person present to apprehend that he who makes that gesture or preparation is about to use criminal force to that person, with the Explanation clarifying that mere words do not amount to an assault, but words may give to gestures or preparations their meaning.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Protects psychological bodily security by penalizing threatening gestures or physical preparations that create an immediate, reasonable apprehension of incoming physical violence.
statutoryFramework: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, BNS s. 130 (corresponding to IPC s. 351).
Actus reus: Making any gesture or preparation in the presence of another person.
Mens rea: Intending or knowing it to be likely that the gesture/preparation will cause apprehension of imminent criminal force.
Explanation: Mere words do not constitute assault; words combined with gestures or preparations give them context and meaning.
Statutory illustrations: Shaking a fist; unmuzzling a ferocious dog; raising a stick.
essentialIngredients: The accused made a gesture or preparation.
The gesture or preparation was made in the presence of the victim.
The accused intended or knew it likely that the act would cause the victim to apprehend that the accused was about to use criminal force.
The victim experienced a reasonable apprehension of immediate criminal force.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 130 defines assault in its strict legal sense, which differs from popular usage (where 'assault' is often confused with battery or beating). In law, assault is the immediate threat of violence, not the violence itself. The actus reus consists of a physical 'gesture' (shaking a clenched fist, brandishing a dagger, raising a cane) or 'preparation' (pulling out a revolver, rolling up sleeves while advancing, unchaining a dog). The mental element requires creating an apprehension in the victim that criminal force is about to be used immediately. An assault cannot be committed over the phone or by a letter, because there is no apprehension of immediate force. The Explanation establishes that mere words alone never amount to assault; however, words spoken during a gesture clarify its threatening nature (e.g., shaking a cane while shouting 'I will break your head').
examples: Teaching example (Shaking fist in face): An accused marches up to a colleague, stops six inches from his face, clenches his fist, draws it back, and snarls 'I am going to knock your teeth out.' This is an assault under s. 130.

Teaching example (Mere words vs gesture): An individual sitting fifty feet away shouts 'I will kill you tomorrow!' No gesture or immediate preparation is made; under the Explanation, mere words do not constitute assault.
distinctions: Assault (s. 130) vs Criminal Force (s. 129): Assault is the threat creating apprehension (inchoate); Criminal force is the actual execution of force (consummated contact/motion).

Assault (s. 130) vs Criminal Intimidation (s. 351): Assault requires immediate physical gestures creating imminent apprehension; Criminal intimidation covers future threats to reputation, person, or property.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an accused who drew a country pistol from his jacket and cocked the hammer while staring at a victim three feet away committed an assault, even though bystanders disarmed him before he fired.
Rule: Making a preparation intending to cause apprehension of imminent criminal force constitutes assault under BNS s. 130.
Application: Cocking a firearm in close proximity is an overt preparation causing immediate terror of lethal force.
Conclusion: The act constitutes assault under BNS s. 130.

Requires apprehension of immediate criminal force.
